extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style and usage guide specifying word choice, capitalization, hyphenation, grammar, measurement and attribution rules for writing Reuters news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship names and pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put quotation marks round the names of ships. Always use neuter pronouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-covering
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-lived / short-sighted
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shutdown
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words, no hyphen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side by side
rubrics_metrics.description: As an adverb, no hyphens (they walked side by side). Hyphenate as an adjective (side-by-side display).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sierra Nevada
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write 'Sierra Nevada mountains' (tautologous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Silicon vs silicone
rubrics_metrics.description: Silicon chips but silicone implants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simla / Shimla
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Shimla, India (not Simla).

rubrics_metrics.name: Since
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'since' to mean 'because'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single out
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only for single examples. Do not use for listing multiple items (e.g. He singled out Britain, France and Italy...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinn Fein/IRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'Sinn Fein/IRA'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siphon
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'siphon', not 'syphon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'situation' can usually be dispensed with (e.g. avoid 'a crisis situation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more specific wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills (jargon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon. Avoid if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skipper
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only of fishing vessels; otherwise use 'captain'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slam (quoted language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang. Prefer 'said' to 'slam'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slang (use in copy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid slang not readily understood outside the English-speaking world or your country. If a vivid quote contains slang, explain it in brackets or paraphrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He’s in the cat-bird seat (in a favoured position) — or paraphrase the quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slew
rubrics_metrics.description: Colloquial and a cliché. If you mean a large number or amount, express it more precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slump (definition/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden or serious fall in economic activity or prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smithsonian Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Smithsonian Institution', not 'Smithsonian Institute'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoulder / smolder
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'smoulder' (British); 'smolder' is American style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sneaked
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'sneaked', not 'snuck'.

rubrics_metrics.name: So as to
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'to' instead of 'so as to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: So-called
rubrics_metrics.description: Used as adjective and adverb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Security
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize when referring to the U.S. system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socialist
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize only when part of a proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software capitalization & quoting
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize software product names without quotation marks (e.g., Windows). Use quotation marks for computer games (e.g., “Bust a Move: Dance Summit”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Somali
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Somali', not 'Somalian'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some (usage with numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'about 500 people' rather than 'some 500 people'. Using 'some' to indicate approximation can confuse translators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song titles capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize every word in the title apart from conjunctions, articles, particles and short prepositions (e.g., 'All You Need Is Love').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophisticated (avoid overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid calling weapon systems 'sophisticated' as a modish word; say 'modern' or be specific instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOS formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'SOS' (appeal for rescue) with no spaces and no points.

rubrics_metrics.name: South Asia (region usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'South Asia' for the region including Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space age
rubrics_metrics.description: The space age began with the launch of Sputnik 1 on Oct. 4, 1957.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space centre / space center
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'space centre' (British), 'space center' (American). Use in stories to describe spacecraft launch facilities; do not use 'spaceport'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaceship / space shuttle
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower case unless part of a proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacewalk
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the word 'special' because it rarely adds value; instead describe what is special.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species
rubrics_metrics.description: Same word for singular and plural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeds (numerals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use numerals for speeds (e.g., 7 mph, 7 to 9 knots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling regional conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two generally accepted spelling systems. Copy originating in the Americas should follow North American spelling; copy originating elsewhere should follow British spelling norms. Always stick to official spellings for American names and titles and watch regional words that may confuse translators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In American sports coverage, use American terms and spellings (e.g., center, maneuver, defense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spill (verb forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'spill, spilling, spilled' not 'spilt'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin off / spinoff
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spin off' is the verb; 'spinoff' is the noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spokesman / spokeswoman
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'spokesman' or 'spokeswoman'; not 'spokesperson'. If the sex of the person is not known then use 'representative'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoonful
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'spoonful, spoonfuls', not 'spoonsful' or 'spoons full'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports events titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower case for sport names (junior, men’s, women’s, championship, tournament, match, race, game etc.). Use upper case for an event title (e.g., French Open tennis championships). Use singular 'championship' when one title is at stake and plural 'championships' for more than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the name of the sport before 'championship', 'tournament' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Think twice before using metaphors drawn from sport — they are often particular to a single sport or culture and difficult to translate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using slang or sport-specific metaphors, explain or avoid (e.g., 'bowling a googly').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sprang / sprung
rubrics_metrics.description: Sprang is the past tense; sprung is the past participle (e.g., Spring has sprung).

rubrics_metrics.name: Square leg / square-leg
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words for the fielding position in cricket ('at square leg'), but hyphenated as an adjective ('square-leg umpire').

rubrics_metrics.name: Stadiums vs stadia
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'stadiums', not 'stadia'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagehand
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stanch vs staunch
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'stanch' for the verb (to stop) and 'staunch' for the adjective (loyal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The staunch supporter stanched the flow of blood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star Wars (SDI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quote marks when 'Star Wars' means the U.S. Strategic Defence Initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Startup
rubrics_metrics.description: One word for a new business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star / superstar
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid these terms; do not use in sports reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: State names (abbreviation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviate the names of U.S. states only in datelines. In text, spell out names in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Station wagon
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary vs stationery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stationary = fixed/still. Stationery = writing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute mile
rubrics_metrics.description: About 1.6 km.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepping stone
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stretcher (noun vs verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'stretcher' as a verb. Use 'was carried off', not 'stretchered off'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stealth (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize 'stealth' when describing aircraft or weapons. See military.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storey / story
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'storey' for floors (British). In American style, 'story' is used for both senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storms (terminology & naming)
rubrics_metrics.description: A storm is more severe than a gale. Terms vary by region (cyclone, typhoon, hurricane, tornado). Meteorological offices name tropical storms; regional naming practices differ. To be recognized as a typhoon winds must be 17 m/s (56 ft/s) or stronger. The Beaufort scale measures wind speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strait vs straight
rubrics_metrics.description: A strait is a narrow channel joining two bodies of water. 'In dire straits' is idiomatic. 'Straight' applies to linear or direct meaning (e.g., home straight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Straitjacket / strait-laced
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Straitjacket' and 'strait-laced' (narrow in principles). Do not use 'straight-laced'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic vs tactical
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve the distinction: strategy concerns conduct of a campaign; tactics concern manoeuvring in presence of the enemy. Do not use 'strategic' to mean merely 'important'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratum / strata
rubrics_metrics.description: One stratum, several strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stricture
rubrics_metrics.description: Means adverse criticism or a binding/closure; adverse criticism is the common meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'strike' as a transitive verb. For strike action say 'strike'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong-arm
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenated as verb and adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub- prefix
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, no hyphen as a prefix (sub...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submachinegun
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also Military.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'subpoena, subpoenaing, subpoenaed' (standard forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subprime
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent to
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'after' or 'later' instead of 'subsequent to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute for / replace with
rubrics_metrics.description: The verb 'substitute' takes the preposition 'for'. Do not confuse with 'replace with' or 'replace by'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successfully (can be excised)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Successfully' can often be removed (e.g., 'They sailed round the world' vs 'They successfully sailed round the world').

rubrics_metrics.name: Such as vs like
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Such as' is used when offering an example. 'Like' means similar to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Players such as Smith, Patel and Jones are essential'; 'Politicians like Brown have short tempers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudan
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Sudan', not 'the Sudan'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super (prefix)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, no hyphen as a prefix (super...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlatives (claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with 'first', 'largest', 'biggest', 'highest', 'oldest' — have a source for such claims and be skeptical of news releases claiming records (especially auction records). Avoid similar value judgments (e.g., 'company giant').

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrounded (tautology)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Completely surrounded' or 'surrounded on all sides' are tautologous; avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUV
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand for Sport (singular) Utility Vehicle (SUV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Swath vs swathe
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'swath' is a strip cut by a scythe; 'swathe' is to wrap or a binding/bandage. Use 'cut a swath' and 'swathe someone'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swat vs swot
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Swat' a wasp; 'swot' for exams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sync / synch
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'sync' to shorten 'synchronisation' (e.g., out of sync).

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize / synthesise
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'synthesise' and 'synthesizer' (British); in American style 'synthesize', 'synthesizer'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'table' as a verb — it has conflicting meanings (to put forward and to postpone discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted (spelling/usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not 'targetted'. Except in military context prefer 'aimed at' or 'directed at', or describe exactly what is being done to whom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid saying the same thing twice (e.g., 'a new record' where 'new' is unnecessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other examples: 'originally built', 'future risks', 'in a westerly direction'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax avoidance vs evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax avoidance is legal; tax evasion is illegal. Be specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teas and temperature formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Express temperatures in Celsius and Fahrenheit, using the scale of the country involved first, with conversion in brackets. Spell out 'Celsius' at first reference, abbreviate to C and F subsequently. Give conversion formulas and examples for above and below zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 20 Celsius (68 Fahrenheit). Use the conversion rules provided for accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temple Mount / al-Haram al-Sharif
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the significance and terminology; Temple Mount is a 14-hectare area sacred to Jews and Muslims and the site of al-Haram al-Sharif.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrorism (labelling & attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: May refer without attribution to 'terrorism' and 'counter-terrorism' in general but do not refer to specific events as 'terrorism' without attribution. Do not use 'terrorist' without attribution to qualify specific individuals, groups or events. Retain 'terrorism'/'terrorist' in direct quotes, but be careful in indirect speech to ensure source attribution. Avoid using inverted commas around 'terrorist' or preceding it with 'so-called'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report subjects objectively, use dispassionate language, and prefer specific terms like 'bomber', 'attacker', 'hijacker'. Use fuller quotes if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: That vs which
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'that' in defining clauses and 'which' in non-defining/informative clauses. Avoid unnecessary use of 'that'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the cup that cheers' vs 'the cup, which was blue, was full of water.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Thai names (second reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first name alone at second reference (e.g., Prime Minister Chatichai Choonhavan ... Chatichai added).

rubrics_metrics.name: There is / there are (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'There are two choices facing the captain' are usually unnecessary; prefer 'The captain faces two choices.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Third World (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the term 'Third World'; use 'developing countries' or 'poor countries' instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time formatting and dateline conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations of time zones are acceptable if GMT equivalent is given. Give local time by the 12-hour clock (without saying 'local time') followed by a bracketed conversion to 24-hour clock time for a specified zone (e.g., 10 a.m. (1600 GMT)). Use figures except for 'noon' and 'midnight'. Use a colon for hours and minutes (3:15 p.m.). Use 'on Friday' rather than 'Friday' in British-style text. Avoid vague phrases like 'several months ago' — be precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles (capitalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize an official's title when it immediately precedes the person's name; when the title follows the name or is used alone, use lower case (e.g., President Tom Smith; the president said).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Military titles for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Told reporters vs told Reuters
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Told reporters' should be used when the source is speaking informally to a group of reporters. 'Told Reuters' should be used only when Reuters is being given significant information or an exclusive; otherwise use 'told reporters' or 'told a news conference'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information is given by telephone and would be available to anyone, use 'the spokesman said' instead of 'told Reuters'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ton / tonne / long ton / short ton
rubrics_metrics.description: Use both 'tons' and 'tonnes' but make clear which kind is meant (long and short where appropriate). Definitions: tonne = 2,204.6 lb (1,000 kg); long ton = 2,240 lb; short ton = 2,000 lb (American). Use 'lb' for pounds in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonnage of ships (units)
rubrics_metrics.description: For passenger liners and most vessels (not warships/tankers/dry bulk cargo) express tonnage in gross registered tonnage (grt). For tankers and dry bulk cargo vessels use deadweight tonnes (dwt). For liquefied gas carriers use cubic metres more often; for container ships use teu or feu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cgt (compensated gross tons) is used in statistics to show shipbuilding capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top (avoid tautology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'top' sparingly as it is often tautological (e.g., 'top aides').

rubrics_metrics.name: Torpedo forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'torpedoes' for plural and 'torpedoing' for the gerund/continuous form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tortuous vs torturous
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tortuous' = full of windings or far from straightforward. 'Torturous' = causing torture. Use appropriately (negotiations are often tortuous, rarely torturous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total wording
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'total of' is usually redundant — just give the figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a brand/symbol/word registered and protected by law. Use a generic equivalent unless the trademark is important to the story. When using a trademark, follow the owner's capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Aspro not aspro but aspirin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trans- hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the second element of a word beginning with 'trans-' starts with a capital, hyphenate (e.g., trans-Siberian). Exceptions: transatlantic, transfat, transpacific, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency (word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Transparency' can be a vogue word; 'openness' often serves as a substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transpired
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'transpired' in the sense of 'came to be known', not 'happened'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation vs transport
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'transport' except where 'transportation' is part of a title (e.g., U.S. Department of Transportation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transsexual / transvestite (sensitive terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'transsexual' as a person identifying or wishing to live as the opposite sex; transvestite is regarded by many cross-dressers as pejorative and should be avoided. Use preferred descriptions of how a person wants to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related guidance on respectful language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trillion (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trillion means one thousand billion. Spell it out (but can be abbreviated to 'trln' in headlines). Always use numerals before 'trillion' (e.g., 2 trillion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triplets (parallel verbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing three items ensure a proper complement of verbs: each element should have its verb (avoid 'Three Iraqis were killed, 22 captured and the crew tried...' — insert 'were').

rubrics_metrics.name: Troop vs troupe
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Troop' = soldiers or a group; 'troupe' = performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Troubled (defamation caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful using 'troubled' to describe entities (especially companies) as it can be defamatory; be specific (e.g., 'the company that lost $4 million').

rubrics_metrics.name: Truck
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'truck', not 'lorry'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try and
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'try to' instead of 'try and'.

rubrics_metrics.name: T-shirt
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'T-shirt', not 'teeshirt'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuberculosis
rubrics_metrics.description: May be referred to as 'TB' at second reference. The adjective is 'tuberculous', not 'tubercular'.

rubrics_metrics.name: TV
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptable contraction for 'television'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twice (pluralization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'twice', not 'two time' or 'two times'. Bigger numbers should be plural (e.g., 'seven times champion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Typhoon capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize when the storm has been given a name (e.g., Typhoon Mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyre vs tire
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'tyre' (British); in American style use 'tire' (on a wheel).

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. datelines and city stand-alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain U.S. cities stand alone in a dateline without the state (e.g., Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, New York, Washington).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the provided list for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Nations (abbreviation & first reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'United Nations' at first reference when used as a noun. It may be abbreviated to 'U.N.' in a headline. As an adjective, it can be abbreviated at first reference (e.g., the U.N. General Assembly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring to U.N. agencies, you may use an acronym after first explanation (e.g., UNHCR).

rubrics_metrics.name: United States (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'United States' in text when used as a noun; may be abbreviated to 'U.S.' in a headline. Do not use 'USA' except in quoted passages. Do not use 'America' as a synonym for the United States (use 'American' as an adjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. legislative titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not abbreviate legislative titles in the United States. Use 'Governor', 'Senator', 'Representative' at first mention and then surname on subsequent references. No need to include the district or state unless essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'senior'/'junior' when referring to a state's senators.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. courts
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain U.S. court system divisions: state courts vs federal courts; federal system consists of district courts, courts of appeal, and the U.S. Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: New York Supreme Court is a trial court; the Court of Appeals is the highest state court.

rubrics_metrics.name: URLs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any style acceptable for website addresses (Uniform Resource Locator).

rubrics_metrics.name: User friendly (jargon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon. Prefer 'easy to use'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilise vs use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'use' rather than 'utilise'.
